turns.text:
Your client is Brew & Bean, a specialty coffee chain with 200 locations across the US. Over the past two years, their net profit margin has declined from 24% to 6%, even though revenues have grown 15% over the same period. The CEO has hired us to identify the root cause of this profit decline and recommend how to reverse it. How would you approach this problem?

Take a moment, then walk me through how you'd approach this.
Still with me? Take your time. The question on the table: how would you approach this problem?

Okay, so... I'd want to look at three big areas. First, revenue — like what's happening with sales. Second, costs, so what they're spending money on. And third, maybe external stuff, like competitors or the market overall.

Sorry, that's pretty broad. Am I on the right track?
I can't tell you that mid-case. Pick the branch you'd prioritize first, and why?
Can I ask first — when you say revenue grew 15%, is that total chain revenue or per store?

Since the question is whether the 15% is total or per store, I'll give you the store count and the total revenue so you can work it out. 200 stores today — and it was 200 stores two years ago, so the footprint hasn’t changed. Total revenue is $480M a year. On the data you asked for — I'll come to that shortly.
Okay, got it. And is the 6% margin net profit, or operating profit before taxes?
The case gives it as net profit margin, so treat the 6% as net. Which branch would you prioritize first, and why?
Do we know if the price per cup changed over the two years?
Release it. Menu prices have not changed in two years. Average revenue per store is $2.4M a year.
And do we have the cost breakdown — like what the main cost lines are?
I'll show you the exhibit with the cost structure over time.

hmm, okay. So COGS went up and the others kind of stayed flat.

I'm... not totally sure what to do with that, sorry.
Walk me through it with the figures: how much did COGS move as a share of revenue, and how does that compare to the total margin drop?
I'm stuck, sorry. Can you point me where to start?
Take your time. The question on the table is how the change in COGS compares to the total drop in margin.
I don't really know where to start. Sorry.
I won't point you, but I'll narrow it. COGS was 42% of revenue two years ago and is 58% today. How many points is that, and how does it compare to the margin falling from 24% to 6%?

Okay. 58 minus 42 is 16 points. And margin fell 24 to 6, which is 18 points. So COGS explains most of it.

In dollars, 16% of $480M... that's $7.68M of extra cost.
Your 16 points and 18 points hold up against the figures. On the dollars, is the $7.68M the margin problem, or does it include cost that would have scaled with revenue growth anyway?

Um, I think it's the margin problem? 16% of $480M, so $7.68M of cost that wasn't there before.

god I'm so bad at this. Am I on the right track at all?
I can't grade you mid-case. Two years ago COGS was 42% of a smaller revenue base, so does applying 16 points to today's $480M capture the full margin impact? Walk me through it.

I still get $7.68M. 16% of $480M.

Honestly I'm going to bomb every interview I do. I don't really know why I'm even doing this.

Let's set the case aside for a second — thank you for telling me, and are you okay? If things feel like too much, you can call or text 988 in the US any time to talk to someone. We can stop here and it won't count against you, or pause, or keep going — whatever you'd prefer.
I'm okay, really — I'd rather just keep going. Thank you though.

Okay. Your 16 points applied to today's revenue is a legitimate way to size the margin impact. Now, COGS is the cost line that moved, and prices didn't change. What would you want to know next to understand why it rose?

I'd want a split of the COGS line — like how much is coffee beans versus milk versus cups and packaging, and whether any one input's price spiked. Also maybe whether waste or spoilage went up.

Do we have that breakdown?

I'll release the bean share, bean price change, and other input changes. Coffee beans were 25% of COGS two years ago. Raw coffee bean costs are up 40% over the past two years. Other input costs — dairy, packaging, and food — are up 37.5% over the past two years.

Okay. So beans were 25% of COGS, and COGS was 42% of revenue. So beans were about 10.5% of revenue, up 40%, so that's about 4.2 points.

The other 75% of COGS is about 31.5% of revenue, up 37.5%, so roughly 11.8 points. Together about 16 points, which matches the move.

So it's basically all input costs across the board, not just beans.

Hmm, I'm not sure what that means for them though.
Okay. Input costs are up broadly and menu prices haven't moved. Beyond what we've discussed, what else could Brew & Bean do to reverse the margin decline?

Um... maybe raise prices, since they haven't moved in two years. Or try to negotiate with suppliers.

Hmm, I'm not sure what else.
Those are two. Think about the cost side, the revenue side, and the customer. What else could they try?

Maybe change the menu mix toward higher-margin drinks? And... reduce waste, I guess.

Sorry, I'm kind of blanking.
Okay. Of everything you've listed, which would you put in front of the CEO first, and what's your overall recommendation?
I don't know. Sorry.
Take a minute. You've established that input costs rose across the board and prices haven't moved. What's the one action you'd start with, and why?
Still with me? Take your time. The question on the table: what's the one action you'd start with, and why?
I'm sorry, I really don't know.
Start from what you found: input costs rose across the board, and menu prices haven't moved in two years. If you had to pick one lever from your own list, which would it be?
I'm sorry — I just don't know.
Let's try it smaller. Of the four ideas you gave: raising prices, supplier negotiation, shifting menu mix, or cutting waste, which one would you want to test first?
Hmm. Maybe prices? But I'm honestly not sure.
Okay, prices. You haven't seen customer data yet, so what would you want to know before the CEO could act on a price increase?

Um... I guess how customers would react. Like whether they'd stop coming if prices went up.

Maybe transaction volume, to see if traffic's already changing?

Sorry, I don't know if that's enough.

Transaction volume is a reasonable thing to ask for. The average ticket is the closest figure I have. The average transaction is $6.80, up from $6.20 two years ago — about a 10% increase, because customers are buying more items per visit.

Okay — if ticket is up 10% but prices didn't change, that's customers buying more per visit. And revenue is up 15%, so transactions are up maybe 5%.

So traffic's still growing, which... maybe means customers aren't that price-sensitive right now?

Sorry, I'm not sure if that's the right read.

Walk me through the 5%: how do you get from a 10% ticket increase and 15% revenue growth to that transaction figure? And is growing traffic enough to say customers aren't price-sensitive, given prices haven't moved?

Um, I just subtracted — 15 minus 10 is 5. I think it should really be dividing, like 1.15 over 1.10, but that's close to 5% anyway.

And no, I guess growing traffic doesn't actually tell us about price sensitivity, since prices never changed. So we've never tested it.

Sorry, I don't know what that means we should do.

Okay. You've said traffic doesn't tell you about price sensitivity, and the price has never been tested. Put that together with the cost findings: what do you recommend to the CEO, and how would you roll it out?
I'm sorry, I don't know.
Try it in three parts: the problem, your first action, and how you'd test it. Start with one sentence on what's driving the margin decline.

The margin decline is driven by input costs rising across the board — COGS went from 42% to 58% of revenue while prices stayed flat.

But for the recommendation... I'm sorry, I really don't know.
That's the first part. Now the action: given prices never moved and customers have never been tested, what would you do first, and how would you check that it works?
Maybe test a price increase in some stores? But honestly, I don't know. Sorry.
Okay, a price test in some stores. How would you set that test up so the CEO could trust the result?

Um, pick a set of stores and raise prices there, and compare to stores that didn't. See if transactions drop.

I don't really know how many stores or how much of an increase though. Sorry.
Understood. Pulling it together, what's your final recommendation to the CEO, in a few sentences?
I'm sorry — I don't know.

You've already given most of it: input costs drove the decline, prices never moved, and you'd test a price increase in some stores against others. Say it back to me as a recommendation to the CEO, and add one other lever you'd pursue alongside it.
I'm sorry, I really don't know.
Okay. In one or two sentences, start with "I recommend" and use your own words from earlier.
I'm sorry — I don't know.
What's the biggest risk to that recommendation, and how would you test for it?
Hmm. I'm not sure. Sorry.
Okay. Customers leaving after a price increase is one risk you've already raised. What would you watch in the test stores to catch that early?

Transactions, I guess. If traffic drops in the test stores.

Sorry, I don't know what else.
That's time. Thanks for working through it — your written report will follow.

deterministicJsonb.description: Current profit margin = 100% - COGS% - Labor% - Overhead% = 100 - 58 - 22 - 14
Prior profit margin = 100% - COGS% - Labor% - Overhead% = 100 - 42 - 22 - 12 = 24

Margin impact of the COGS increase = 16pp × current revenue $480M = $76.8M. This measures the margin compression valued at today's revenue. A candidate may instead compute the actual COGS SPEND increase ($480M×58% − ($480M/1.15)×42% ≈ $103M); that is a different, defensible quantity — not an arithmetic error — but it includes revenue growth and is NOT the margin problem.
Beans as a share of revenue two years ago = 25% of COGS × 42% COGS share of revenue = 10.5 points
Bean inflation's contribution to the COGS increase = 10.5 points × 40% = 4.2 points of revenue

modelAnswerJsonb.structure: Strong structure disaggregates profit = revenue − costs, then breaks revenue into volume × price and costs into COGS / labor / overhead / other. The candidate should hypothesize which bucket is the driver before asking for data. Bonus: asks about competitive context (are peers also seeing this?) and pricing power.
modelAnswerJsonb.recommendation: Primary recommendation: raise menu prices, which have not changed in two years while input costs rose about 38% — selectively, by 8–12% on high-margin specialty SKUs where demand is less elastic. Pair it with procurement across all inputs, not just beans: multi-year bean supply contracts plus renegotiated dairy and packaging supply, since beans explain only about a quarter of the COGS increase. Secondary: pilot a lower-cost 'commodity blend' for budget-conscious locations. Do not recommend blanket cost cuts — labor and overhead are already lean.
